title: Probe Deprecation and Slice Retirement Policy
author: Maya Patel
body:
Overview:
This page defines the lifecycle and operational process for retiring evaluation probes, deprecating prompt slices, and removing obsolete benchmark artifacts from Redwood's eval catalog. The goal is to reduce annotation cost, avoid noisy probes, and keep the probe catalog aligned with production workloads while preserving auditability and reproducibility.

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to: all probes (unit probes, probes used by shadow validation, and synthetic probes) and prompt slices defined in sources/confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/prompt-sets-and-benchmarks.
- Excludes: legal/compliance-labeled probes and customer-specific private probes unless explicitly requested by the customer.

Principles:
1) Safety-first: retire only when quality signal and telemetry indicate low utility or active harm.
2) Reversibility: maintain a rollback window and archived snapshot for at least 90 days.
3) Cost-benefit: retirement must reduce annotation or eval-run cost by >= 20% or remove probes that cause repeated false positives.
4) Traceability: every retirement has an associated change record with owner, rationale, and dataset snapshot.

Definitions:
- Probe: an individual test case / request used by the eval harness.
- Slice: a named grouping of probes (e.g., long-context, negation, multi-turn).
- Retirement candidate: a probe or slice flagged by telemetry or steward review for deprecation.

Signal sources that trigger deprecation:
- Telemetry: low hit-rate (<2% of active probe runs across last 90 days), persistent flakiness (>15% variance in pass rate vs. cohort), or causing >5% of eval pipeline failures.
- Annotation economics: maintenance cost > $X /month (projected) for low-impact probes.
- Model evolution: probe no longer relevant because model capability changed (e.g., tokenization differences) and cannot be remediated.
- Redundancy: high semantic overlap with other slices (overlap score >0.85 in fingerprinting).

Process: step-by-step retirement workflow
1) Identification (Owner: Probe Steward)
   - Create a Retirement Issue in the eval board with: probe ids, slices affected, telemetry summary, and initial recommendation (retire, merge, or rewrite).
2) Triage (Owner: Stewards + Applied ML lead) — 5 business days
   - Review telem. If candidate meets at least two trigger conditions, schedule for archival review.
3) Archival review & stakeholder notification — 7 business days
   - Notify: owners of dependent evals, annotator leads, product manager owners.
   - Publish "Retirement Notice" to eval-stewards channel containing impact matrix.
4) Shadow validation (optional) — 10 business days
   - Run a shadow pass with the probe removed. Validate that primary eval metrics do not change beyond tolerated delta.
5) Deprecation window — 21 days
   - Mark probes/slices as DEPRECATED in the catalog metadata and UI. They remain runnable but flagged.
6) Final retirement and archival
   - If no objections, retire after the deprecation window: move artifacts to archive, update eval manifests, and add an immutable changelog entry.
   - Archive retention: snapshot of probes and annotations stored in S3 with path pattern: s3://redwood-eval-archive/<year>/<slice>/

Rollback and restoration:
- Restoration request: open a high-priority ticket referencing the retirement changelog id. Restoration requires owner approval and re-run of regression smoke suite.
- Automatic rollback condition: if post-retirement monitoring detects a regression > defined regression-impact-index threshold (see table below), re-instate the probe and alert SLA owners.

Monitoring and acceptance criteria:
- Regression-impact-index table (used to decide automatic rollback):

| Signal | Threshold | Action |
|---|---:|---|
| Delta SQC (service quality contract) median | >= 2.5 points | Auto-rollback + incident page |
| Downstream FPR increase | > 1.5x baseline | Flag for urgent restore review |
| Production user-facing error rate attributed to eval | > 0.2% | Pause retirement, escalate |

Metadata and tagging standards:
- Every retirement issue must include tags: retired_by, retire_reason, telemetry_hash, dependent_evals (comma-separated ids), archive_path.
- Catalog fields to update on deprecation: status=deprecated, deprecated_at=YYYY-MM-DD, deprecation_note=short rationale.

YAML example: Retirement manifest (for automation)

---
probe_ids:
  - p-2024-0891
  - p-2023-4422
slice: long-context-question-paraphrase
reason: low-hit-rate;high-overlap
owner: @maya.patel
deprecated_at: 2026-02-20
archive_path: s3://redwood-eval-archive/2026/long-context-question-paraphrase/
rollback_window_days: 90
---

CLI commands (examples):
- Flag probe as deprecated:
  eval-catalog update --id p-2024-0891 --set status=deprecated --note "low hit-rate; will retire 2026-03-14"
- Generate retirement snapshot:
  eval-ops snapshot --manifest retirement-manifest.yaml --out s3://redwood-eval-archive/2026/long-context-question-paraphrase/

Roles and responsibilities:
- Probe Steward: owns identification and initial issue creation.
- Applied ML lead: triage and final approval for deprecation.
- Annotator lead: provides cost impact estimate and annotation retention requirements.
- Product owner: signs off when probe affects product-facing metrics.
- Release engineering: applies automated catalog updates and archiving steps.

Audit and compliance:
- Keep changelog entries for all retirements with: retire_reason, telemetry snapshot, reviewer list, and archive path.
- For privacy-sensitive probes, ensure anonymized annotation snapshots and follow the data-retention policy before archiving.

Metrics to track success of retirement program:
- Reduction in active probe count (%) per quarter
- Annotation cost savings ($) attributable to retirements
- Number of accidental regressions requiring restores within 90 days

Appendix: Example retirement rationale template (to be included in Retirement Issue)
1) Summary: 2-3 sentence summary of why this probe/slice is proposed for retirement.
2) Telemetry: last 90-day hit-rate, variance, failure contribution.
3) Overlap analysis: fingerprint similarity to other probes (numerical score).
4) Cost estimate: monthly annotation + maintenance cost.
5) Stakeholders: list of teams and expected impact.
6) Proposed timeline: identification -> deprecation -> retirement -> archive.
